newsitem.title: UK: TABLE TENNIS-CHINA CHASE TITLE DOUBLE.
newsitem.headline: TABLE TENNIS-CHINA CHASE TITLE DOUBLE.

text.p: China retained the women's team title and reached the final of the men's event at the world table tennis championships on Tuesday to stay on course to repeat their 1995 clean sweep of all seven titles.
The women, led by Olympic and world champion Deng Yaping, defeated North Korea 3-0 to capture the Corbillion Cup for the 11th time in 14 consecutive final apearances.
In the men's event, China saw off South Korea 3-1 to reach their 13th final in the last 14 championships, while France edged Germany 3-2 to make the final for the first time.
The Chinese, who have won the title 11 times since their first appearance in 1961, did not have things all their own way, world champion Kong Linghui suffering his second successive defeat.

Kong lost to Sweden's 1989 world champion Jan-Ove Waldner in Monday's quarter-finals. This time the 20-year-old world number one succumbed to South Korea's 1988 Olympic gold medallist Yoo Nam Kyu 21-18 10-21 21-18 in 40 minutes.
Fortunately for China, world number six Wang Tao was successful in both his visits to the table.

Wang, the left-hander with the hardest hit in the game, destroyed Oh Sang-Eun 21-12 21-7 in just 15 minutes. If it had been a fight the referee would have stepped in to protect his opponent from further punishment.
But Wang, playing in his fourth world championship, had a tougher task against world number five Kim Taek Soo, winning 21-12 16-21 21-17.
Earlier, Kim had lost the opening match 21-14 22-20 against China's Atlanta Olympic gold medalist Liu Guoliang.

Team coach Cai Zenhua was confident about Sunday's final in the light of China's quarter-final victory over second-seeded Sweden and Tuesday's success against the Koreans. "Sweden and South Korea were our biggest threat to winning the Swaythling Cup for the 12th time. We have cleared our biggest barriers, the heavyweights, and now we are going to take on the lightweights," he said, indicating he did not care whether France or Germany were in opposition on Wednesday. "China have more good players than Germany and France put together."
But he ruled out any complacency in the Chinese camp. "I have to put my players on high alert. Any mistake or act of failure can prove very costly."

France and Germany had a battle royal with Germany's Olympic bronze medallist Joerge Rosskopf carrying the fight by winning both his matches, against Damien Eliol and 1991 world champion Jean-Philippe Gatien.
Fortunately for the French, Gatien, Damian Eliol and Patrick Chila all managed to win one match which spelled the difference between success and failure.
The highlight of the two-and-a-half hour clash was the battle between Gatient and Rosskopf which the German eventually won 21-13 16-21 21-19 after trailing 14-9 in the decider.
That made the match score 2-2. But Rosskopf's rescue act proved in vain as Eliol won the decider against Steffan Fetzner.
